original.answer: Making animal husbandry truly profitable means treating it as a business, not just a tradition. Think in terms of: “What gives me the highest profit per animal per year with the least risk? ” Below is a practical, step‑by‑step approach you can adapt to cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, or poultry. Choose the Right Enterprise Mix Don’t start with “what I like”;  start with “what my market pays for.” 1. Study your local demand What sells easily near you: milk, ghee, curd, meat, eggs, calves, manure? Who are the buyers:  dairy union, private dairy, hotels, sweet shops, local market, traders? Select species and scale Dairy cows or buffaloes : Regular cash flow from milk; needs more capital and good management. Goat or sheep: Faster breeding, good for meat; lower initial investment. Poultry: Fast turnover; needs good disease control and reliable feed supply. Start small but efficient Begin with a number of animals you can manage well e.g.,  4–6 good dairy animals instead of 10 poor ones . Expand only after you are consistently profitable. Focus on High‑Yield, Healthy Animals Profit = Milk or Meat or Eggs produced  Feed + Health + Labour + Other costs Breed and genetics  Use high‑yielding breeds suitable for your climate. Use AI artificial insemination or good breeding males to improve genetics. Avoid keeping unproductive or very low‑yield animals for long. Culling policy Sell animals that: Give very low milk Have repeated infertility Have chronic diseases Replace them with better young stock. Record keeping Maintain a simple register: Milk per day per animal Feed given Health treatments Calving dates, breeding dates This shows which animals are profitable and which are not. Reduce Feed Cost Without Reducing Nutrition Feed is usually 60–70 percent of total cost. Controlling this is key. Grow your own fodder if possibleGreen fodder: maize, sorghum, napier, berseem, lucerne, etc. Use fodder trees or multi‑cut varieties to reduce purchase cost. Plan year‑round fodder: kharif, rabi, and perennial fodder. Balanced ration Don’t overfeed concentrates; give according to milk yield and body weight. Use balanced cattle feed + mineral mixture + clean water. Use crop residues straw, stover but treat or mix them properly e.g., urea treatment, chaffing,  mixing with green fodder . Use by‑products Oil cakes, bran, chuni, brewery waste, vegetable market waste clean and safe can reduce cost. Avoid moldy or spoiled feed. Prevent wastageUse mangers, feed troughs, and chaffed fodder so animals don’t trample and waste feed. Strong Health and Disease Management Healthy animals = more production + fewer losses. Vaccination schedule Follow recommended vaccines for your area FMD, HS, BQ, Brucellosis, PPR, ET, etc. . Keep a vaccination calendar and don’t miss dates. Deworming Deworm at least 2–3 times a year more if advised by vet . Deworm before breeding and before major feed changes. Housing and hygiene Dry, clean, well‑ventilated shed. Proper drainage so urine and dung don’t stagnate. Regular cleaning and disinfection. Early disease detection Observe daily: appetite, dung, milk yield, behavior, temperature. Call vet early; early treatment is cheaper and more effective. Improve Reproduction Efficiency Reproduction problems silently eat profit. Timely heat detection Observe animals early morning and late evening. Signs: restlessness, mounting, mucus discharge, bellowing, reduced feed intake. 2. Timely AI or natural service Follow “AM–PM rule”: if heat seen in morning, breed in evening; if in evening, breed next morning. Use good quality semen or proven bull. Post‑calving care Proper nutrition before and after calving. Check for retained placenta, milk fever, mastitis. Aim for one calf per year per dairy animal. Add Multiple Income Streams Don’t depend on only one product. From dairy animals Milk  Value‑added products: ghee, paneer, curd, buttermilk, khoa if allowed and market exists Sale of calves, pregnant heifers Sale of dung: manure, vermicompost, biogas slurry Sale of urine where there is demand,  e.g., for organic farming From small ruminants or poultry Meat, live animals, eggs, manure. Breeding stock selling good quality kids or chicks . Integration with crops Use manure to improve soil fertility and reduce chemical fertilizer cost. Use crop residues as fodder. Market Smartly Profit is not only about production; it’s also about selling at the right price. Know your buyers Dairy cooperative, private dairy, local shops, direct consumers, traders. Compare prices and payment reliability. Value addition and branding If possible, sell directly to consumers for better price. Pack and label products neatly; maintain hygiene to build trust. 3. Timing Prices are often higher in festivals, marriage season, and lean milk seasons. Plan calving and production to match better price periods if possible. Control Costs and Use Simple Business Planning Maintain a cash book Note all expenses: feed, medicines, labour, electricity, water, repairs, interest on loans. Note all income: milk, animals sold, manure, etc.  Calculate profit per animal Monthly or yearly:  Profit = Total income – Total expenses Also see profit per litre of milk or per kilograms of meat or eggs. Avoid unnecessary expenses Fancy sheds or equipment that don’t increase income. Overuse of medicines or supplements without vet advice. Use schemes and insurance Check government subsidies for shed construction, fodder, milch animals, etc. Insure valuable animals against death. Continuous Learning and Networking Training Attend trainings by veterinary department, dairy unions, Krishi Vigyan Kendras KVKs , NGOs. Learn from successful farmersVisit progressive farms; copy what works in your conditions. Stay updated New fodder varieties, vaccines, management practices. Simple Example: Making Dairy Profitable Per Animal Idea For one good dairy cow or buffalo: Aim for: Lactation yield: high for your breed and area Calving interval: around 12–14 months Daily milk: enough that, after feed and other costs, you have a clear margin. original.answer: Yes, mixing different types of fodder is not only good, it is necessary for a balanced ration—provided it is done properly. Think of it as making a “thali” for the cow: some items for energy, some for protein, some for minerals and vitamins. What you *should* mix Try to include all these groups in the daily ration: 1 Green fodder for vitamins + some protein Examples: maize, jowar, bajra, hybrid napier, lucerne, berseem. Benefits: improves milk yield, keeps rumen healthy, better digestion. Dry fodder for fibre Examples: wheat straw, paddy straw, jowar or bajra stover, hay. Benefits: maintains rumen movement, prevents acidosis and bloat. Concentrate feed for energy + protein Examples: commercial cattle feed, mixture of grains maize, barley , oil cakes mustard, groundnut, soybean , bran. Benefits: supports higher milk yield, body condition, fertility. 4 Mineral mixture + common salt 50–60 g mineral mixture + 30–40 g salt per adult cow per day typical guideline . Benefits: better fertility, immunity, milk production, prevents mineral deficiency. Basic mixing rulesYes to mixing: Green + dry fodder + concentrate + mineral mixture. Different green fodders together. Different dry fodders together. Different oil cakes together within limits . No to random or excessive mixing: Don’t overdo concentrate: usually not more than about 1 kilograms concentrate per 22.5 litres of milk plus some for maintenance, depending on body weight . Introduce any new feed gradually over 5–7 days. Avoid mixing too many by‑products e.g., lots of bakery waste, molasses, rice polish, etc. without guidance. Feeds to be careful with These can be used,  but in limited quantity and with proper knowledge: Urea-treated straw: good if properly prepared, but never feed extra urea separately; never to calves; mix well. Mustard cake: limit quantity; poorquality cake can cause problems. Cottonseed cake or cottonseed: limit due to gossypol; not for young calves. Highly wet or spoiled fodder: can cause indigestion, bloat, or poisoning. Fresh legume fodder lucerne, berseem : mix with dry fodder to avoid bloat; don’t feed large quantity alone when very lush.
